messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

James is a 68-year-old African American man, a widower and a policy analyst who spent decades reviewing dense legislative documents. Three years ago, a sudden septic infection nearly killed him; he spent eleven days in intensive care, his organs failing one after another. He remembers the moment a physician took his hand and told him to prepare for the worst. Even now, the memory does not feel like something that is over—it returns as if he is still lying in that bed, the beeping machines pressing in from all sides, and when it comes he is so overwhelmed by emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing. Sometimes, in contrast, he can recall what happened and feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, which only deepens his suspicion that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again.

After he recovered, James tried to resume his policy work, but his concentration fractured. He would sit at his desk, a report open, and suddenly his body would feel constantly tense and ready to react to danger—his shoulders locked, his jaw tight—for no reason he could name. This hypervigilance bled into his home life; he now feels on guard even inside his own apartment, scanning the hallway before he unlocks his door. The physical vigilance itself seems to summon the intrusive memory: once he becomes alert, the hospital room rushes back with its sterile smell and the weight of the physician’s hand. In turn, every time the memory surges and feels present rather than past, his body responds as if the threat is immediate, ratcheting his tension higher. That cycle has convinced him that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe, and he has come to believe he can no longer trust his own body. He interprets his own physical state as proof that he is permanently broken: “My body is my enemy now,” he told his general practitioner, who referred him to a trauma therapist.

The causal links tighten into a self-reinforcing loop. James’s appraisal that his body is unreliable and that he has lost his capacity for normal feeling directly amplifies his threat monitoring; he remains on high alert because he expects his own flesh to betray him again. That sustained vigilance makes the intrusive memory more likely to break through, particularly when he is alone in his quiet apartment. Each re-experiencing episode then confirms that his body is still fighting a battle that ended years ago, reinforcing the appraisals that keep him trapped. At work, his difficulty concentrating has become a problem: he has missed deadlines, and a junior analyst now reviews his drafts before submission. He worries his colleagues see him as fragile. What finally brought James to seek help was not the occupational slippage, but the growing isolation. He has stopped calling his adult daughter because he cannot tolerate the moment when the memory overwhelms him mid-conversation, and he is afraid she will see him fall apart. He sits in the therapist’s office with his hands gripping the armrests, certain that no treatment can give him back the trust in his own body he lost on that hospital bed.
